title: Spot eviction buffer sensitivity playbook (routing policy draft)
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an experimental playbook and cost-sensitivity model for using an eviction buffer (short-lived reserved capacity / prewarm pool) to reduce user-visible latency and relaunch churn when routing requests away from spot instances during evictions. It is intentionally a working doc: heuristics, rough spreadsheets, and next steps for product/infra experiments.

Executive summary / recommendation (TL;DR):
- Maintain a small regional eviction buffer sized to cover the expected short tail of spot evictions (suggested starting range: 3–8% of steady-state GPU capacity per region) and prefer on-demand fallback only after buffer exhaustion.
- Use an adaptive buffer policy keyed on recent regional eviction rate and request-SLA tier: premium routes keep a higher buffer, background/noisy batch workloads use more aggressive spot fallback to save cost.
- Run A/B experiments with 1) static buffer (3%, 5%, 8%), 2) eviction-rate adaptive buffer (EWMA lookback 30m/3h), 3) no buffer + instant fallback, measure cost delta, tail latency, and relaunch failure rates for 2 weeks.

Why this matters:
Spot instances are cheap but introduce two classes of cost/fragility not present with on-demand: (1) eviction-induced relaunch cost (requeueing work, KV cache warm-up, retried requests hitting on-demand), and (2) tail latency from capacity reallocation. An eviction buffer trades a small steady-state cost premium for reduced relaunch churn and better tail latency. We need a simple, observable policy so customers can opt-in and we can reason about unit economics across regions.

Key definitions and assumptions used in the model (spreadsheet tabs referenced):
- steady_capacity_gpus: number of GPUs expected under normal load (tab: assumptions).
- spot_cost_per_gpu_hour: current market average for spot in region (tab: pricing).
- on_demand_cost_per_gpu_hour: baseline on-demand price.
- eviction_rate: fraction of spot capacity lost per hour (observed), typically 0.5%–4% hourly depending on region/time-of-day.
- relaunch_penalty_per_eviction: cost of replacing a machine beyond direct price (recompute time, KV cache warm-up, extra tokens billed, failed request retries). We start with $35 per GPU-eviction as a placeholder (explained below).
- buffer_size_fraction: fraction of steady_capacity kept as buffer (e.g., 0.05 = 5%).

Simple expected cost formula (sheet: model_simple):
Expected hourly cost = (steady_capacity_gpus * ((1 - buffer_size_fraction) * spot_cost_per_gpu_hour + buffer_size_fraction * spot_cost_preference))
+ E[evictions_per_hour] * relaunch_penalty_per_eviction
+ fallback_costs_when_buffer_exhausted
Notes: spot_cost_preference: buffer can itself be spot-backed preferrably with quicker prewarm heuristics (warm AMIs, cached model shards). If buffer uses reserved/dedicated instances for faster warm-start, replace spot_cost_preference accordingly.

Eviction-impact breakdown (intuition):
- If eviction_rate is low and relaunch_penalty is high, small buffers pay off.
- If eviction_rate spikes above threshold (empirically ~6–8% hourly), buffer size must scale rapidly; otherwise fallback to on-demand is cheaper.

Sample sensitivity table (output from quick simulation in tab: sensitivity_sample):

Parameters: steady_capacity=200 GPUs, spot=$0.30/hr, on-demand=$1.10/hr, relaunch_penalty=$35 per eviction.

Buffer | Effective steady spot share | Estimated hourly cost | Est. evictions/hr | Expected relaunch cost/hr | Total/hr
3%     | 97%                       | $69.3                | 4 (2%)            | $140                      | $209.3
5%     | 95%                       | $68.1                | 4                 | $140                      | $208.1
8%     | 92%                       | $66.1                | 4                 | $140                      | $206.1
No buffer | 100%                    | $72.0                | 4                 | $140                      | $212.0

Interpretation: with these placeholders the difference is small in absolute dollars but buffer options reduce variance in tail latency and relaunch frequency; effects amplify with higher relaunch penalties and higher evictions.

Regional routing interaction notes:
- Each region needs its own buffer parameter; eviction dynamics vary by region and by cloud zone. We recommend per-region EWMA eviction metrics and buffer sizing driven by a policy that maps EWMA(eviction_rate) -> buffer_fraction via a piecewise linear curve (configs stored in Console / rollout policies).
- Cross-region fallback should prefer nearest region that still meets SLO and has buffer headroom; add a hop-cost penalty for cross-region data egress and cold KV misses.

Spot vs on-demand fallback orchestration heuristics (policy sketch):
1) Primary attempt: route to spot-backed pool.
2) If spot pool signals eviction pressure (EWMA centered) and buffer headroom above threshold, shift new requests to buffer-prepped machines (same region).
3) If buffer exhausted or eviction_rate > failover_threshold, fallback to on-demand or dedicated pool.
4) When relying on on-demand, keep a small windowed probe to re-insert spot capacity to capture reclaimed savings.

Operational telemetry and SLOs to track (sheet: telemetry):
- eviction_events_by_region (count/hr)
- buffer_fill_pct and buffer_warm_success_rate
- tail latency (p95, p99) pre/post-eviction window
- relaunch_retry_count and failed_restarts
- cost_per_inference_token rolling 24h

Experiment plan (two-week cadence):
- Week A (baseline): current policy (no explicit eviction buffer), collect 7d metrics.
- Week B1: static buffer 3% in two regions (us-east1 and eu-west1) for 7d.
- Week B2: adaptive buffer (EWMA alpha ~0.2, min 2%, max 10%) in same regions for 7d.
Track: cost delta, p99 latency delta, failed restart rate, and perceived customer impact (errors, increased API latencies).

Customer-facing knobs and console UX ideas:
- Slider: "eviction buffer (recommended)" with tooltips showing estimated monthly cost and tail-latency improvement for chosen regions.
- Toggle: per-environment (dev/stage/prod) defaults and per-route override for SLO tiers.

Open questions and assumptions we need to validate quickly:
- Relauch_penalty_per_eviction: $35 is a placeholder. Need an infra experiment to instrument true end-to-end cost per eviction: retry token consumption, extra billing, and human ops time. (Linked sheet: cost-decomp tab).
- Buffer warm strategy: should buffer use instant-on dedicated nodes or prewarmed spot instances? The former increases steady cost but reduces warm time; latter preserves savings but increases eviction coupling.
- How long should we keep buffer instances idle before returning them to the pool? Policy: keep warm for 15m by default, configurable by route.

Immediate next steps (owners):
- Product (Maya + Rhea): finalize experiment design and feature flag gating. (Due: 2025-11-25)
- Infra (Ethan + Samir): instrument eviction_event_cost metric and a sandbox patch that can simulate buffer sizes cheaply. (Due: 2025-11-20)
- Analytics: create sample cohort queries in the linked sheet and onboard the experiment dashboards.

Appendix: quick math notes (how relaunch penalty was estimated):
- average in-flight request tokens lost per eviction: 12k tokens -> avg cost on retry: $0.004 (placeholder)
- KV cache warm-impact: additional 30s of CPU/GPU under-provisioning translates to 0.008 GPU-hr of extra work per eviction (~$0.002 at spot).
- ops/human time allocation per high-severity eviction incident amortized across customers -> $20 contribution.
- combine above with secondary lost-request SLA credits -> round up to $35.

If this doc reads like it’s missing details, it is on purpose — the goal is to seed the experiments and capture pragmatic heuristics.

Questions/feedback welcome in #optimize-eviction-playbook or drop comments in the linked sheet.
